This column is resting size, not executed size. A 🐋 is a limit order sitting there — an offer, which can be pulled. The number beside it is how long it has held, and that is the part that tells you something. A whale that has rested 60s+ is real defence someone is willing to show. One that appears and vanishes within a few seconds is spoofing — bait to make you think support exists. Watch what happens when price actually arrives: absorbed and holding is real, gone before it trades is not. On Auto, the bar is 5× the median resting size or 8% of visible depth, whichever is higher, so ordinary levels never qualify. For executed size, use Block Flow.

This is order-flow pressure, not a trade signal. It reads what size is doing right now across nine live inputs — it has no view on trend, structure or where you'd put a stop. The horizon is minutes. Two inputs are deliberately contrarian: an overheated basis and a lopsided top-trader book both count against the crowd. When the components disagree, the mixed reading is the information; a needle near centre means genuinely no edge, not a mild one.

Two different measurements, deliberately. Total flow comes from exchange klines and is complete and exact for any window, including time before you connected. Biggest individual prints can only come from the live trade stream, so that list starts when you connect and fills as the session runs — the coverage note tells you how much of the window it actually has. Nothing is fabricated to fill the gap.

Read the last column. It shows where price sat 10 seconds after each print. PUSHED — the order moved price its own way, it met no resistance. ABSORBED — price barely moved, someone was sitting there taking the other side. FADED — price went the opposite way, the strongest form of absorption. Repeated big buys getting absorbed or faded is distribution into strength; repeated big sells absorbed is accumulation into weakness. Rows are sorted biggest first, not newest first. Verdict threshold is 0.03% over 10s.

Evidence at this price — every line is measured, none is inferred
Phone alerts. When a setup confirms the terminal also posts it to the collector, which forwards it to Telegram and WhatsApp if you have those configured. It says sent to your phone below the verdict when that succeeds, and stays quiet when no collector is running. Note that the gate itself runs in this browser, so these only fire while the terminal is open somewhere — the collector's own liquidation and cascade alerts are the ones that reach you with the laptop shut.

It watches on its own — you never need to press RESCAN. While a proposal is still valid the gate keeps scanning, and swaps to a materially stronger level if one appears. Turn on 🔊 ALERT and it chimes the moment a setup confirms: a rising three-note tone for a long, falling for a short. The card flashes, and the browser tab title changes so you see it even from another tab. It fires once per setup, and stands down by itself when the setup stops being confirmed. A confirmation must hold for a few seconds before anything is sent, and the same level cannot alert again for five minutes — so a verdict flickering on the edge of a threshold is one alert, not a stream of them.

In AUTO the terminal picks the level itself and keeps it only while it is still valid. Candidates come only from measured structure — resting walls that actually exist, liquidation clusters that actually fired, and the volume profile's edges. Each is scored on the same checks and the best across both directions wins, so the gate also tells you which side is the better trade right now. Ranking counts the live-flow checks double, so a level with something actually happening at it outranks one that has merely collected context.

A proposal clears itself when price runs more than 1.2% past it (missed), breaks 1.2% through it (level failed), a blocker holds for thirty seconds, or it is more than ten minutes old — then it immediately picks a fresh one and says what happened to the previous. Switch to MANUAL to pin your own level instead.

It still has no opinion on your thesis. It reports whether anything measurable is actually at a price. CONFIRMED means price is in your zone, nothing is against you, at least five checks support the side you chose, and — the part that matters — at least two of the three live-flow checks pass: resting size in the zone, aggressor flow over five minutes, and what large prints are doing. The other checks are context. A level can collect all of them and still be worth nothing, so context alone can no longer confirm anything; if flow cannot be read the gate says so instead of confirming. WAITING means either price has not arrived yet, or it has and the evidence is thin — those are different and the subtitle says which. INVALIDATED means something measured is actively against you; the blocking line is highlighted.

It now has a map, and the map can veto. Every check before this looked at one price through a microscope — what is resting here, what is trading here, what got liquidated here. None asked which way the market is going or whether this price is a cheap place to buy. The record shows what that cost: the gate has fired long far more often than short and the longs have done worse, and every confirmation in the first recorded session was a LONG, in a market that fell all afternoon, with aggressor flow reading weak on every one. The micro evidence was real. The direction was wrong.

Three questions are now answered from the gate's own klines, on its own timeframes, independent of any dropdown you might change. HTF structure: whichever came later, a 15m close above a prior swing high or below a prior swing low, is the direction structure last committed to. Premium / discount: where the level sits between the swing high and swing low that bracket price, with the midpoint as equilibrium. Liquidity sweep: whether a pool was run and reclaimed — both halves, because a level broken and held is a break, not a raid.

The first two are vetoes, not extra points. A long into a clean bearish break is refused; so is a long priced above equilibrium. Under the old scoring, enough order flow at one price could outvote the direction of the entire market, and it did. Candidates now include untapped swing highs and lows, the reclaim level itself, and the 0.62–0.79 retracement of the range — levels a top-down trader would have marked in advance, rather than only artefacts of the current book.

And it now checks whether the raid actually worked. Seeing a sweep is not a setup — stops get run constantly and price carries on in the same direction most of the time. What separates a raid from a continuation is what happens next: a candle that displaces, closing through the opposing swing point with a body at least 1.2× the recent average range, leaving an unfilled gap behind it. That is the market-structure shift, and until it happens there is no evidence the traders who were just filled are in trouble. This was the last blind spot: the card used to say the lower-timeframe trigger was left to you, which meant the gate could confirm a setup whose entire premise — this reversal has begun — was unverified.

Four states are distinguished. No raid on this side, nothing to confirm. Stops run but nothing displaced yet — the reversal has not started, so the setup waits. Structure shifted, with the size of the candle and the level it closed through. And the raid failed: price closed back through the level it swept, which means the move was real after all — that one is a veto, because the premise is now known to be false. The unfilled gaps those displacements leave are offered as levels in their own right, since they are the part of the move nobody got filled in and the entry the method actually names.

Expect it to refuse far more, including whole sessions. A bearish market sitting at the bottom of its range vetoes both sides: longs fight structure, shorts are selling cheap. That is the correct answer and it used to be a signal.

The ratio is quoted NET, and that is the whole change. The gate used to price a setup against a stop it assumed would hold exactly and a fill it assumed would happen at the level. Its own record says neither is true: across every Entry Gate trade that has stopped out, the average loss is −1.68 R, not −1.00 R — price clears the level between prints, and on a 0.6% stop one aggregate trade can do it. The control arm overshoots identically, so this is the instrument and not the signal. At −1.68 R a loss against +1.30 R a win, break-even is a 56% hit rate, not the ~40% the quoted geometry implied, and the gate was passing setups that could not pay for themselves.

So R:R is now computed from where the fill would actually happen, against a stop widened by a slippage factor the gate measures from its own closed trades, minus the 0.10% round trip. Until ten stops have been recorded it assumes ×1.35; after that it uses the real number, clamped so a handful of trades cannot run away with it. A gross 1.50:1 — which the old rule passed — comes out at 0.88:1 net and is blocked; passing now takes about 2.15:1 gross. Expect far fewer confirmations, and expect that to be the point.

The entry is priced where you would be filled, not where the level is. The zone is ±0.20% wide, which on a 0.5% stop is forty per cent of the risk. One recorded win came in at +0.38 R on a setup the gate had passed as better than 1.5:1, because by the time price reached the zone the target was nearer than the stop. Once price is inside the zone the live price is the entry, and if the stop or target has ended up on the wrong side of it the setup is dead rather than merely thin.

The stop and target are derived, not advice. Both come from the nearest liquidation cluster that carries real weight and sits between 0.15% and 3% away — near enough to be this trade's structure, big enough not to be dust. If nothing qualifies the card says so and falls back to fixed distances, which is steadier than borrowing a cluster from somewhere else. The stop sits beyond the nearest real liquidation cluster, because that is where stop-hunting pays. The target is the nearest opposing resting liquidity, because that is where price is likely to stall. If the resulting R:R is poor, the honest conclusion is that the level is wrong — not that the stop should be tightened into the cluster.

None of this is validated against outcomes yet. These checks are reasoning about measured data, not a backtested edge. Log what happens before you size up.
🧮 State & Probability — five layers, then a measured number LIVE
TARGET STOP WITHIN Matched across many perps' candle histories, shrunk by independent sample size. Book and tape history do not exist publicly, so those layers are recorded live instead.
The five layers are the live state. Aggression (market buys and sells, delta, CVD, imbalance), resting liquidity by distance (±0.1, ±0.25, ±0.5, ±1%), what is being consumed, cancelled or reloaded, positioning (open interest, funding, liquidations, price-versus-OI), and how price is responding (displacement in ATR, volatility, volume expansion, VWAP, range position). Each is read from the panel that already measures it, so nothing here can disagree with the rest of the terminal.

The probability is a frequency, not a score. It takes the part of the state that public history can carry — trend, volatility regime, volume expansion, displacement, distance from VWAP, position in range, taker-buy share, and positioning from open-interest history (its 1-hour change, and whether that change agreed with price, which is the difference between new money and a squeeze) — matches it against the histories of the most liquid perps rather than this one pair, and counts what happened next: reached the target before the stop, or not. Three defences against flattering itself: neighbours from the same coin inside the same half hour count as one observation, since overlapping bars are not independent; the raw rate is shrunk toward the base rate by that independent count, so a lucky run of ten cannot print as 80%; and every figure is also given as expected R after 0.10% fees, because 60% at 2:1 and 60% at 1:2 are opposite trades. A candle that touches both barriers counts as a coin flip, and if that happens often the panel tells you the barriers are too tight.

The learned model is a logistic regression over the same pooled rows, trained on one set of coins and scored on coins it never saw, with a reliability curve — when it says 70%, did 70% resolve? If it cannot beat the base rate out of sample it is not shown at all, and the panel says so. A model that fails honestly is worth more than one that is quietly displayed.

Your recorded states is the part no public history can give you. Binance keeps candles, not order books or tape, so the five layers are snapshotted live once a minute and their outcome attached afterwards from candles. That database starts empty and grows while the terminal is open; below 300 resolved snapshots it reports only the count, with no borrowed confidence. Once it fills, it is the only estimate here that has actually seen order flow.
⚖ Order Flow Imbalance — what the book does, not only what the tape did LIVE
CVD counts aggressors. This counts the book. Every addition, cancellation and execution at the best quotes is signed and summed — price up on the bid adds its size, price unchanged adds the change in size, price down subtracts what was there, and the mirror on the offer. That is the net pressure the book itself applied, including the passive side that trade data cannot see. The top five levels are included with deeper ones weighted down, since depth away from the touch is cancelled far more freely than it is filled.

Why this measure and not another. Work on Binance perpetuals across coins from large to small finds order flow imbalance the most important single predictor of near-term returns, ahead of spread and VWAP deviation, with a roughly monotonic relationship that flattens at extremes. That finding is about OFI as a feature; it is not a promise about any particular horizon.

Two numbers on this card, and they are not the same number. The impact row regresses each second's OFI against that same second's move. It is a contemporaneous fit: it explains the second it happened in and forecasts nothing. Published replications score that specification at R² ≈ 0.40 — and score the genuine one-second-ahead forecast, on the same data, at 0.03. A factor of thirteen separates the description from the prediction, and only the second one can be traded. The Forecast power by horizon table is the predictive one: OFI now against the return after it, fitted on the first 70% of the window and scored on the 30% it never saw, with the t-statistic computed on non-overlapping windows so that six hundred overlapping five-minute paths are not counted as six hundred observations.

Read the decay, not the headline. The row where the numbers reach zero is the horizon past which this book has nothing to say. The published evidence places OFI's power in seconds: a 2026 study of Binance perps targets a three-second return, and the quarter-hour work targets the following ten seconds. A signal scored over five or ten minutes is being scored far outside the window where this measurement has ever been shown to work, and a flat table is a normal reading rather than a fault.

The quarter-hour windows. A 2026 study of six Binance perpetuals documented algorithmic execution clustering at :00, :15, :30 and :45, with imbalance measured in the first seconds after those boundaries predicting returns four to twelve hours out — while the same measurement at other times carried little. The terminal records that window on every boundary, scores it against this pair's own previous boundaries, and logs anything beyond 1σ to the Outcome Tracker at its longest horizon. It is listed as a signal to be measured, not a rule to follow: if it does not pay on your pairs, the tracker will say so.
📏 Move Length — how far a direction travels, and where the target stops paying LIVE
Direction is the easy half. A correct call with the target in the wrong place still loses, which is exactly what your confirmed turns did — right read, wrong geometry. Distance is a first-passage problem, so it is measured as one, over the same comparable historical states the direction engine uses.

Survival and hazard. The REACHED column is the survival curve: how often the matched states got that far before giving back 0.75 ATR. The next column is the hazard — given it already came this far, how often did it go one step further. That is the number that answers the question you actually ask on the screen. A hazard that falls as distance grows is the mathematical statement of "do not chase"; one that holds up is a trend worth trailing rather than capping.

Target by expected value, not by hope. For every candidate distance, EV = P(reach) × R − (1 − P(reach)) − costs, with R measured against the 0.75 ATR invalidation. The highlighted row is the target that maximises EV, shown in ATR, in R and as a price. It is usually nearer than instinct suggests, because the tail of the distribution is thin and you pay the full stop to chase it. FURTHER is the median and upper-quartile extra travel of the states that did get there, which is what makes a runner worth leaving on rather than a target worth moving.

Two properties of the pair itself. The variance ratio over 5-minute returns says whether moves currently extend or fade here: above 1 they follow through, below 1 they revert, with the Hurst exponent given as the more familiar name for the same thing. The branching ratio comes from the Fano factor of trade counts and estimates how much activity is the market reacting to itself rather than to outside news — near 1 is a crowded feedback loop where cascades run long, low means flow stops when the news stops.

What this is not. It is not a forecast, and nothing here is calibrated. It is a conditional distribution with its sample size attached, and like every other estimate in this terminal, its real test is whether the calls built on it resolve the way it said.
🛡 Risk Governor — the part that says no ARMED
DAILY LOSS CAP MAX OPEN PER COIN CALLS / DAY COOL OFF AFTER
This panel does not have an opinion about the market. It counts what the day has already cost, what is already at risk, and how the last few calls went. When a limit is reached it adds a failed hard gate to the A+ card and refuses to open new calls until the clock or the UTC day resets. Everything else keeps running: setups are still graded, signals still logged, the tracker still resolves them. It stops you trading, not the tool from measuring.

Why the limits are in R, not dollars. One call is one R of risk by construction — size comes from the stop — so a tight stop on a quiet coin and a wide one on a violent coin cost the same when they fail. That makes a daily cap meaningful across coins. The caps: total loss for the day, risk open at once, calls per day, one position per coin, and a cooling-off period after a losing streak, which is when traders do most of their damage.

It is enforced in two places — the gate on the A+ card, and the call ledger itself — so a setup cannot slip through while the panel is folded. Switching Enforce off disables it entirely and the badge says OFF rather than pretending to protect you.
⭐ A+ Setup — the only one worth taking IDLE
EQUITY $ RISK % MIN R:R BAR MAX RISK
One answer, not twelve panels. This card grades the Entry Gate's current evaluation against everything else the terminal measures, and shows a tradable setup only when nothing is against it. Hard gates are pass or fail: the gate's own confirmation (HTF structure, premium / discount, a raid that displaced, two of three live-flow checks), net R:R at your minimum after slippage and fees, no confirmed footprint turn against the trade in the last 15 minutes, the Hunter not reading this coin as extended or the other way, a tradable spread, and optionally a regime that is not chop. Two of those gates came out of your own results rather than theory: a stop wider than the max risk cap is refused, because a wide stop is not a smaller position but a different trade — every wide-stopped confirmed turn in the first sample resolved at −1R, several after 10R of favourable travel; and a setup pointing against the measured probability for its direction is refused, so the probability panel holds a veto rather than a vote. Miss one and the answer is NO SETUP, with the missing one named.

Only A+ becomes a call. When a setup is A+ and holds for a few seconds, the terminal opens a CALL on the coin it is on — entry, stop, target, size and the ingredients behind it — and one call at a time per coin, so the card never talks over itself. It is then tracked to a result: live price while you are on that coin, and Binance 1-minute candles whenever you are not, including after a reload, so nothing is lost and nothing is scored against the wrong pair. Stop and target in the same minute count as the stop; untouched after 60 minutes it expires at the price then. Results are net of the 0.10% round trip, in R.

Those calls are what teaches it. Each ingredient's measured lift — average R with it present minus without, taken from the resolved calls themselves — pulls its weight up or down, shrunk by sample size so a handful of trades cannot rewrite the book. Ingredients still on their reasoned prior say prior; earned ones show their lift and the number of calls behind it. One prior has already been cut on evidence: the live-flow ingredient dropped from 1.2 to 0.7 because across 6,400 recorder records the flow read finished behind its own same-moment control, 61 wins to 97 in the pairs where they disagreed. Until ten calls have resolved the weights borrow from the wider Outcome Tracker pool, and the card says so. Nothing is hidden: if an ingredient is being down-weighted, you can watch it happen.

Size is yours, not advice. Position size comes from your equity and risk percentage against the setup's own stop, with the round-trip fee shown in R so a setup whose costs eat the edge is obvious. Early on, expect NO SETUP most of the time, and expect the weights to be nearly meaningless until a few dozen setups have resolved. That is the honest state of it — the card gets sharper as the Outcome Tracker fills, not before.
📈 Chart — candles with everything this terminal measures on them TRADINGVIEW ENGINE
TF Everything the terminal measures is drawn on these candles.
Two charts, because they answer different questions. L2 CHART runs on TradingView's Lightweight Charts engine, bundled into this file so it works with no network beyond Binance. It is ours to draw on, so it carries the terminal's own work: the live A+ call with its entry, stop and target, past calls marked where they ended and at what R, footprint turns with their scores, the Entry Gate's proposed level, the volume profile's POC and value area, the heaviest liquidation clusters near price, and the Hunter's range. Delta sits in its own pane. The forming candle follows the live tape between fetches, so it never lags the book beside it.

Footprint cells replaces the candles with the footprint itself — the same bars, numbers, imbalances, stacked shelves, value areas and POC path as the footprint card, with its profile down the right edge, each bar's delta and volume under it, and cumulative delta in its own pane. Everything else on this chart keeps drawing over it: calls, turns, zones, liquidation clusters and prints. The tape only reaches back as far as this session, so the view frames what exists rather than stretching a few cells across days of candles; switch it off and the candles and their full history come back.

What is drawn. Calls and their levels, footprint turns, the Entry Gate level, POC and value area, liquidation clusters and the Hunter's range — plus the structure zones the gate takes its candidates from (order blocks, fair-value gaps, untapped pools, the OTE bands), the volume profile down the right edge with its value area and POC marked, forced liquidation prints on the candle they hit, control shifts from the footprint's own bars, per-bar delta in one pane and cumulative delta in another. Each has its own switch. Everything is read from the same functions the original panels use, so a box here and a box there can never disagree. Freehand drawing tools stay in the footprint's CELLS view and on the TradingView tab — the engine has none of its own.

TRADINGVIEW is the real tradingview.com chart embedded — every drawing tool and indicator you know, and none of ours. Their widget is a sealed iframe: no third party, this terminal included, can draw inside it. That is their restriction, not a shortcut taken here, and the only way around it is TradingView's Advanced Charts library, which has to be applied for and self-hosted with your own data feed. Use the embed for classic technical work and switch back here for the terminal's evidence.

🧠 Auto Analysis — the whole read in one panel READY
chart builds when the panel opens
Connect and open this panel — it reads candles on demand.
Everything here is computed, nothing is asserted. Each line comes from a named calculation on closed candles of the selected timeframe. The developing bar is excluded from every indicator, pivot and level, so a reading cannot change after the fact — what the panel says at 10:04 is what it said at 10:00, and the swing points it uses are only the ones that were already confirmed by the pivot rule at that time.

The levels. Support and resistance are built from confirmed swing highs and lows, clustered together when they sit within a fraction of ATR of each other, and then ranked by how many independent reactions each cluster has, how recent they were, and how far price was rejected. Only the two strongest bands either side of price are shown, as bands rather than lines, because that is what they are. The Fibonacci grid is anchored to the most recent confirmed major swing and the anchor itself is printed above it; the 61.8% level is highlighted when price is near it and is not treated as a reversal in its own right.

The order book line is not buyer dominance. Resting bids and asks are orders that have not traded. They can be cancelled, they are routinely placed to be seen, and a thick bid is as often a seller’s backstop as a buyer’s intent. The panel reports the imbalance because it moves price in the very short term, and labels it as resting size rather than as demand. Executed aggression is a different measurement and lives in the Flow Meter and the footprint.

Why it so often says wait. The verdict needs trend, momentum, structure and volume to agree. Most of the time they do not, and the honest output then is that there is no edge rather than a direction with a confidence number attached. The scores are not win probabilities and are not labelled as such: they are counts of how much of the evidence currently points one way, which is a different and much weaker claim.

The candles are live, the analysis is not. The right-hand bar is the one still forming, updated every second from the traded price, so the chart is never frozen waiting for a close. Everything measured from it is a different matter: the moving averages, RSI, MACD, ADX, the swing points, the bands and the Fibonacci anchor are all computed from closed candles only, and the forming bar is excluded from every one of them. That is the only way a level written down at 10:04 still reads the same at 10:59, and it is why the panel can be trusted to have said what it says it said.

The view is yours. The chart fits itself to the data once, when you change coin or timeframe, and never again. Zoom and pan survive every refresh; the FIT button puts it back when you want it back.

What is drawn, and why that and nothing else. The chart carries only objects that came out of the calculations on its right: the three moving averages, the Fibonacci grid with its anchor, the two support and two resistance bands as price lines, and the confirmed swing points labelled higher-high, higher-low, lower-high or lower-low. Volume sits under the candles, then RSI with its 30/50/70 guides, then MACD with its signal and histogram. Nothing is drawn from a pattern name or a guess, and every line disappears the moment the calculation that produced it stops holding.

What it does not do. It will not size a position or place a stop — the A+ Setup card already owns that, with the risk governor behind it — and it does not read open interest or funding into the verdict beyond reporting them, because those are positioning, not direction.

A cell reading Positive describes the last few candles; it does not forecast the next ones. What the table is for is the job a single chart cannot do — showing you whether one coin disagrees with the rest of your list, or whether the whole list is leaning the same way, in a glance instead of forty minutes of flicking between charts.

FINAL POSITION is a vote, and the count is printed next to it. Six directional readings, one vote each; ATR and price are not votes because one is a size and the other is a fact. Long and Short need five of six; anything less reads Lean or Neutral. The count matters because these seven indicators are all built from the same closes — they agree most of the time whether or not they are right, and in a chop they will agree and be wrong together. Six out of six is one opinion stated six times, not six opinions.

Closed candles only. The developing bar is dropped before anything is calculated, so a cell cannot change after you have read it. Ichimoku's cloud is the projection drawn 26 bars ago, which is the whole indicator — computing it off today's bar gives a different and wrong answer.

Where it fits. This is the shallow-and-wide view; Auto Analysis is the deep-and-narrow one on a single pair, and Flow ranks the whole market by open interest rather than by indicators. Click any row to load that symbol into the terminal.
🌊 Market Flow — where positions are being put on, across every perp IDLE
Not running.
FLOW UP
press START
FLOW DOWN
press START
Price alone cannot tell you whether money is going on or coming off. Price with open interest can, and the four cases are the oldest classification in derivatives. Price up on rising OI is new longs. Price up on falling OI is shorts buying themselves out — the same green candle, a very different trade, because one has fuel behind it and the other is the fuel being spent. The same split applies downward.

One request, two series. /futures/data/openInterestHist returns open interest in contracts and in dollars, so their ratio is the mark price at that timestamp. A single call per symbol therefore gives the OI series and the price series on identical timestamps — both sides of the classification measured over exactly the same window, with nothing to align. That endpoint costs zero request weight; it has its own allowance of 1000 calls per five minutes, and the sweep is paced at half of it. Sweeping every listed perpetual takes nothing from the rest of the terminal.

Ranked by z-score, not by percentage. Rank five hundred perps by raw OI change and the board fills permanently with the thinnest contracts on the exchange — a coin with $2M of open interest moves 8% when one desk opens a position. Every reading is scored against that symbol's own distribution of changes over the past forty hours, using median and MAD so a single historical spike cannot flatten the scale. A symbol under 0.8σ on both axes reads FLAT, which is the honest answer for most of the board most of the time.

Funding and taker share are the two columns a stock screen cannot have. Long build-up with funding climbing and takers buying is a crowded long paying rent to stay on. Long build-up with flat funding and takers selling is size being absorbed into passive bids. Same cell in the table, opposite trades.

Size arrives in BTC and leaves in alts, so most of what you see is BTC twice. A coin up 3% while BTC is up 3% has done nothing of its own. OWN on each card is the coin's move with beta times BTC's move taken out of it, measured over the ribbon's window — what is left is the part somebody bought this coin for. β is how much of BTC it normally carries. LAGS BTC is where the correlation peaks when BTC's returns are pushed back five, ten or fifteen minutes: a coin that answers BTC two buckets later is one the move has not reached yet, and RANK BY not reached yet sorts the board on exactly that.

ANCHOR is the row that says where the money is. BTC's own state, its share of all the open interest on the board and how that share has moved, and which sector gained the most open-interest value against which lost the most — in dollars, start of window against now. A falling BTC share with dollars arriving in a sector is rotation, stated plainly rather than inferred from a chart.

The data check is not a promise, it is a measurement. This whole panel rests on open-interest value divided by open-interest contracts being the mark price at that bucket. On the first pass the panel fetches the live mark price and the live open-interest reading and compares both against the last bucket, then prints what it found next to the request counter. A five-minute-old bucket should sit a few hundredths of a percent from the mark; if it does not, the line turns red and says so instead of drawing something that looks fine.

RANK BY “unusual for itself” answers a different question from the rest of this panel. It is the mean of the capped absolute z-scores across what the sweep knows about each coin — its open-interest change, its price change, the part of its move BTC does not explain, and its funding against the board. High means out of character, in either direction, and says nothing at all about which way. A coin can top that list for being unusually quiet while everything correlated with it moves. Treat it as somewhere to look, never as something to take: ranking by strangeness finds strange things, and most strange things are not opportunities.

This is triage, not an edge. Open-interest buckets are five minutes wide — the exchange's floor, not a choice made here — and the leaders get a live reading on top of that. Crypto OI is public and continuous, and other tools publish build-up boards; nothing here front-runs anyone. What it does is cut five hundred perpetuals down to the handful that moved significantly against their own history. Click one and it loads into the panels that can actually judge it.
🌡 Volatility Scanner — every perp, by how much it is actually moving OFFLINE
Start it and every listed perpetual is ranked by live realised volatility.
Idle.
One stream, no request weight. Everything here comes from !ticker@arr, which carries last price, the 24-hour high and low, quote volume and trade count for every listed perpetual about once a second. Live volatility is built from that price sequence, so the scanner costs nothing against the rate limit however long it runs.

Live volatility, not yesterday's. RV is the realised volatility of the chosen window — the square root of the summed squared log returns, as a percent. It is what the coin is doing now. 24h range is the day's envelope, and the two disagree constantly: a coin that gapped eight hours ago still shows a wide range while sitting perfectly still. That is why the default ranking is the live figure.

The volume floor is the most important control on this card. Remove it and the ranking becomes a list of the most illiquid coins on the exchange, every single time, because a book that moves 3% on four thousand dollars of flow outranks everything tradable. Vol/$1M makes that visible directly: a high reading there is a thin book, not an opportunity. Avg print separates size from churn — the same turnover looks very different at $40 a print and $4,000 a print.

It needs a moment to mean anything. Live volatility is accumulated from the stream as it arrives, so the window fills in real time and the coverage figure says how full it is. A fifteen-minute reading two minutes in is two minutes of data, and the card says so rather than presenting it as fifteen.

This ranks movement, and nothing else. High volatility is not a direction and not an edge; it is where the stops are wider and the fills are worse. Nothing on this card has been scored against outcomes.
✂ Gap Quality — was the displacement real? OFFLINE
Open and connect to grade the live gaps.
Waiting for data.
This grades the gap at creation, not at the retest. The Footprint card already answers the second question — open its Zones and a gap reads DEFENDED, SOLD THROUGH or UNTESTED by who was aggressive inside it when price came back. This panel answers the first one: whether the candle that tore the gap open was actually aggression.

Aggression comes from the kline, not the tape. Binance publishes taker-buy quote volume on every candle, so taker sell is the subtraction and each closed bar's delta is measurable for the whole history — including the hours before you connected. A +0.60 reading means 80% of that bar's volume lifted the offer. The sign is flipped for a supply gap, so a high score always means the gap's own side was the aggressor.

Shelf is the one measurement that needs your session. Stacked imbalances are a tape measurement, and the tape only reaches back to the moment you connected. When the creating bar is older than that, the row says so and its weight is spread across the other five rather than scored as zero — a measurement you do not have is not a bad measurement.

What the grade is not. It is a description of the candle, not a probability. A gap formed on heavy one-sided aggression is a gap somebody was willing to pay for; it is not a gap that has to hold. Read it as the difference between a level with evidence behind it and a level that only looks like one on a chart — and take the entry from the Entry Gate, which is still the panel that has to agree.
🔭 Timeframe Alignment — whether the clocks agree, and which one is arguing READY
Open this panel while connected — it reads six timeframes on demand.
One question, six clocks. Most losing trades on a good signal are the right read on the wrong timeframe — a clean 5-minute long taken into a 4-hour downtrend, with the stop sitting exactly where the higher timeframe was always going to come back for it. This panel asks the same five questions of every timeframe at once and shows where the answers stop agreeing.

What each column measures. Trend is the 20-period exponential average against the 50, which is the plainest statement of which way the clock is pointing. Structure reads that timeframe’s own swing points: higher highs with higher lows is bullish, lower highs with lower lows is bearish, and anything mixed is a range — the same break-of-structure logic the Entry Gate uses, applied at six scales. Range is where price sits inside that timeframe’s recent high-to-low, stated in the premium and discount language of a dealing range, so a long in the top quarter of a 4-hour range is flagged as what it is. VWAP is price against the volume-weighted average of the last fifty bars on that clock. Volume compares the current bar to the median of its own timeframe, which is how you tell a move with participation from a drift.

The score weights the slow clocks heavier. A daily and a one-minute vote are not the same vote. The bar across the top is the weighted balance of all six, and the sentence above it names the timeframe that disagrees with the rest — because that one is usually the one holding the level your stop is behind.

It is a context panel, not a signal. Alignment across six timeframes is common at the end of a move and rare at the start of one, so a perfect score is not a reason to enter. Read it the other way round: as the thing that tells you which direction you are allowed to take a signal in, and how much room the higher clock will give you before it argues.
📐 Reference Levels — the prices the rest of the market is already watching READY
Connect and open this panel — it builds from candle history on demand.
Magnets around price —
Why these prices and not others. A level matters when enough other people are looking at it, and the set below is the set almost every desk, bot and funding sheet has on screen: the volume-weighted average price of the session with its standard-deviation bands, yesterday’s high, low and close, last week’s high and low, today’s and this week’s opening prints, the first hour’s range, each session’s own high and low, and the points of control left behind by previous days. None of it is proprietary and none of it is clever. That is exactly why it works: these are the prices where resting orders actually sit.

VWAP and its bands. VWAP is the session’s average fill price, so it is the line that decides whether the average participant today is in profit or not — which is why desks measure execution against it and why it behaves as support in an uptrend and resistance in a downtrend. The bands are one, two and three standard deviations of traded price around that average, so they say how stretched the session is rather than how far price has moved: a touch of the second band is roughly a two-sigma excursion from the day’s own mean, not a fixed percentage. Anchored VWAP restarts the calculation from one event — the week’s open, the last swing, the last large liquidation — and answers a different question: what did everyone who traded since that event pay.

Naked points of control. A day’s point of control is the price where that day did most of its business. When price leaves it behind and has not traded back through it since, it is naked, and the panel tags it so. Untested value is the cleanest magnet on a chart because the auction left unfinished business there; a POC that price has already revisited has been resolved and is tagged accordingly.

The first hour. Initial balance is the range of the first sixty minutes of the UTC day. Markets that break it and hold tend to trend for the session; markets that fail back inside tend to rotate between its edges. The panel reports whether it is broken and in which direction, which is the one piece of session context that changes how every other level should be traded.

Distance in ATR, not only in percent. Every magnet is measured both ways. A level 0.4% away is far on a quiet pair and nothing on a volatile one; the ATR column makes that comparison honest, and it is the number to use when deciding whether a target is reachable inside the horizon you are trading.
🧮 Crowd vs Size — derivative history, and whether the gap has paid here READY
Open and connect — history loads on demand.
Binance keeps 30 days of positioning history. Nothing is fetched until this panel is open.
Measured on this coin's own history —
Two different crowds, measured against each other. Binance publishes three positioning series and they are not the same population. Top trader positions is size-weighted across the largest accounts — where the money is. Top trader accounts counts those same accounts one vote each. Global accounts counts every account on the exchange, which in practice is retail. The existing Positioning panel compares the first two against each other, size against head-count inside the top cohort. This panel compares the top cohort against everyone else, which is the comparison people mean by smart money versus the crowd.

The gap, not the level. A 60% long reading means nothing on its own — some coins sit permanently long. What carries information is the spread between what retail holds and what size holds, scored against the same coin's own recent distribution with a median and MAD rather than a mean and standard deviation, so one liquidation cascade in the lookback cannot bend the baseline.

And then the honest part. The table below is not a claim that the gap works. It takes every bar in the loaded window, computes the gap score from a trailing window only — no future data in the score — and reports what actually happened over the chosen horizon, bucket by bucket, next to the same-direction control: the base rate across all bars. If the extreme bucket does not beat its control, the gap is not paying on this coin at this period and the panel says so. Overlapping forward windows inflate the raw count, so the sample is reported as an effective size of roughly one independent observation per horizon, and the Wilson interval is computed on that, not on the raw count. The position is taken at the close of the bar after the one that produced the score, because the exchange publishes these series on a lag and a test that fills at the snapshot’s own timestamp is measuring a price nobody could have got.

What else is on the chart. Open interest with its notional value, taker buy share from the kline's own taker-buy quote volume, funding rate history, and the perpetual basis against the index — the same six series as the exchange's own panels, on one time axis, so a divergence in positioning can be read next to whether open interest was being built or unwound while it formed. Thirty days is the exchange's limit on the positioning series, not a choice.
🎯 Session Recorder — is this terminal actually right? IDLE

SIGNAL VERDICT LOGGEDOPEN WINDOWS / ALL HIT RATE (95% CI) WITH / VS TREND PAIRED vs CONTROL NET / SIGNAL AVG BESTAVG WORST
Every panel here states something falsifiable. The Entry Gate says a level will hold. The Flow Meter says one side is pressing. Block Flow says size is being absorbed. The Liquidity Map says a band is defended or swept. This records each claim at the moment it is made, freezes the price at that instant, and follows it forward.

How each is scored. Entry Gate confirms resolve on whichever comes first, its own stop or its own target — no clock, and unreached in 30 minutes counts as expired, not a win. Flow Meter and Block Flow resolve on price 5 minutes later, Liquidity Map bands at 10 minutes. AVG BEST and AVG WORST are how far the call went right and wrong before it resolved — a signal with a good hit rate but a punishing worst excursion is one you cannot actually hold.

WINDOWS is the sample size, not LOGGED. Signals of the same type that open while an earlier one is still running are the same market moment counted twice. In one recorded session the band signals had a median gap of one second against a ten-minute horizon — five real observations wearing the clothes of five hundred. Everything is still logged, but the interval is computed on the number of non-overlapping horizon-length windows the signals actually occupy, counted per symbol: two signals a minute apart on different pairs are two looks at the market, two on the same pair are one.

Windows are counted off the timestamps, not off elapsed time. An earlier build divided first-to-last by the horizon, which counted every hour the terminal was shut as evidence. A 44-hour export containing 4.7 hours of actual recording was credited with 505 windows where there were 49, and all four rows were marked trustworthy when none qualified. The header now reports recorded time, and the column shows how far the sample is from the ~400 windows it takes to separate a ten-point edge from chance.

NET / SIGNAL is the number that becomes money. Hit rate cannot settle anything for a signal that runs a stop and a target: an Entry Gate hitting 42.9% with wins averaging +0.53% and losses −0.47% is near break-even, not a failure. So the panel reports the average realised move per signal after 0.10% round-trip taker fees, in R where the signal carries its own stop, with a t-statistic computed on the window count. Fees barely move a hit rate and they dominate expectancy, because the average move per signal has been running under 0.05% while the round trip costs 0.10%.

Nothing is discarded. Records trimmed from the live log move to an archive that the statistics and both exports read, so the sample only grows. One earlier export had already destroyed 2,478 resolved observations before anyone looked at it.

The control is matched, not merely parallel. Every signal spawns one control a random 10 seconds to 3 minutes later, carrying its direction, its horizon and its stop and target distances, and the control now records which signal spawned it. That turns two separate populations into matched pairs, so the market, the coin, the direction and the regime are held constant by construction and the only thing left varying is the moment the terminal chose. Pairing also needs far fewer observations than comparing two independent groups, which matters when a session yields sixty windows rather than four hundred.

PAIRED vs CONTROL is the number that decides it. It is the average difference in realised move between each signal and its own control. Because both sides pay the same round trip, fees cancel in the difference — a positive figure is an edge net of costs by construction. Beside it: the 95% interval, the p-value, the number of independent pairs, and how many pairs the signal won where its control lost against the reverse. Pairs are thinned to non-overlapping ones per symbol first, and the win/lost counts feed McNemar's test — exact binomial under 60 discordant pairs, where the chi-square approximation invents significance.

Four signals are tested, so the threshold is tightened. Four independent shots at a 5% bar give roughly a one-in-five chance that something looks significant purely by luck, and reporting the best of four without adjusting is the most common way a backtest fools its author. Holm–Bonferroni is applied across the four, stepping down from 0.0125.

VERDICT is deliberately hard to earn. REAL requires all four of: ten or more independent windows, twenty or more matched pairs, a paired difference that survives the multiplicity correction, and positive expectancy after fees. Anything short of that reads UNPROVEN with the specific requirement that is missing — because "not yet shown" and "shown to be worthless" are different claims, and early on only the first one is true.

The 95% interval is the number that matters, not the hit rate. If the interval straddles 50% the signal is indistinguishable from a coin flip however good the headline looks. Green means the whole interval sits above 50%; red means it sits below, which is its own kind of information.

WITH / VS TREND splits the hit rate by whether the call agreed with the last five minutes of price. A signal can be right about pressure and still lose for an hour by pointing into a running move — the first session issued 440 shorts into an 8% rally, and without this column that reads as a broken signal rather than a trend-fighting one.

Reads that claim nothing score as flat — NEUTRAL and BALANCED cannot be right or wrong, and counting them as wins would flatter every number here.

DOWNLOAD FULL SESSION is the one to send for analysis: every scored signal plus the settings that produced them, the recorded book, the per-second tape, liquidations, block prints, cluster-accuracy samples and any errors — in a single JSON. Heavy series are thinned to keep the file sendable, and the file states exactly what was thinned. Telegram credentials are never included. The CSV and SIGNALS JSON buttons export just the scored signals if that is all you need.

VS CONTROL is the number to trust. A hit rate cannot tell a good signal from a kind week — two sessions on different pairs in different regimes are not comparable, which made every earlier "improvement" unattributable. So every directional signal now schedules a shadow fired into the same market a little later, carrying the same direction, the same horizon, and for the Entry Gate the same stop and target distances, scored by identical rules. Regime hits both arms equally, so the gap between them is the terminal's own contribution. Positive means the moment it chose beat an arbitrary nearby moment with the same bias. Around zero means the signal is picking a side and nothing more. It stays greyed until 25 controls have resolved.

One session is a hypothesis, not a result. Running the same search over these logs with the outcomes shuffled turns up four spurious "edges" of ten points or more every time, purely by chance. Nothing here should change a threshold until it has survived a second session on a different pair.

What this is not. It is not a backtest and it is not P&L. It measures whether price moved the way a signal implied over a fixed horizon, with no fees, no slippage, no position sizing and no execution. A 60% hit rate here does not mean a profitable strategy. What it is good for is comparison: run it across sessions, and when a threshold changes you can see whether the change helped rather than guessing.

Records survive a page reload via this browser's storage, and follow the symbol they were taken on. A record whose symbol was switched away, or whose page was closed, before it resolved is no longer lost: it is re-scored from Binance's own 1-minute candles and the first trade at its resolve moment, never against the wrong pair or a later price, and tagged resolved_via = candles in the CSV. Download before you clear browser data.
📐 Outcome Tracker — which signals actually pay IDLE
HORIZON SOURCE —
SIGNAL VERDICT LOGGED RESOLVED WIN (95% CI) 1R FIRST 2R FIRST EXPECTANCY AVG MFE AVG MAE AVG RISK
This is where every score in the terminal gets checked. Hunter PRIMED and IGNITING calls and every footprint turn are logged the moment they fire: turns once on detection (TURN watch) and again on confirmation (TURN ABS / EXH / CAP ✓), so you can see whether waiting for confirmation actually pays. Each is resolved from Binance 1-minute candles at 15 minutes, 1 hour and 4 hours, wicks included, even if the page was closed in between.

How a result is scored. The stop is the signal's own invalidation: the turn's extreme, the far side of the Hunter's 12h range, or half an ATR back inside the range for an ignition. The target is +2R. Whichever is hit first decides it; if neither is, the trade is marked at the horizon close. When the stop and target fall in the same minute, the stop is assumed first. 0.10% round-trip fees come off every result in R.

When to believe it. Signals on the same coin within 30 minutes count as one look at the market. A verdict needs 20 of those looks; before that it says COLLECTING. EDGE means positive expectancy with t ≥ 2. Then check two things: that higher score buckets resolve better than lower ones (otherwise the score is not ranking anything), and which ingredients show positive lift. That lift table is the evidence for changing a weight. Everything is stored in this browser; export the CSV for your V5 journal.
🗺️ Liquidity Map — real book depth over time OFFLINE
WINDOW BAND HEAT API — —
thin moderate heavy very heavy wall buy print sell print absorbing swept untested wall green can = LONG fuel (below price) red can = SHORT fuel (above price) more cans = more resting size scroll = zoom price · drag = pan · double-click = reset
This is the real book, recorded. Every second the terminal takes the 500-level depth snapshot it already polls and paints it as one vertical stripe. Colour is resting USD size at that price. Scrolling left is history — where liquidity actually sat, not a model.

A bright band that persists is real size someone is willing to defend. It is the same order still sitting there second after second. A band that vanishes without price reaching it was pulled — bait, not defence. A band price traded through and that then disappears was consumed: that liquidity is spent and no longer supports anything.

Volume dots are executed trades, sized by USD and coloured by aggressor — green lifted the offer, red hit the bid. Dots piling up into a bright band that does not fade is absorption: someone large is filling without moving price. Dots at a band that then goes dark is consumption, and price usually continues.

Volume bars along the bottom are traded USD per second, split buy against sell.

Absorption or a liquidity hunt? Both look like heavy trading at a level. The terminal separates them by what the resting size did while it was being hit, and marks the result on the chart. ABSORBING — volume went through and the size is still there (55%+ of its peak): someone is filling passively and not letting price past. SWEPT — heavy volume and the size collapsed below 25% of its peak: that liquidity has been taken out and the fuel is spent, which is what a stop hunt leaves behind. WALL — size still sitting there, barely traded into: untested, and it tells you nothing until price arrives.

This is measured, not inferred. It reports what the size did; it has no opinion on who did it or why, and a level can flip from absorbing to swept in seconds.

Limits worth knowing: depth is sampled once per second, so an order placed and pulled inside that second is invisible. The map starts when you connect — it has no history from before that. Only the visible price band is recorded, so a wall far from the touch will not appear until price approaches it.
👣 Footprint — who traded, at which price OFFLINE
BAR PRICE STEP IMBALANCE STACK WIDTH ENGINE PROFILE —
Who is aggressing and who is absorbing appears here once the tape starts.
What happened after each heavy level traded appears here once there are enough closed bars.
sell imbalance (left number) buy imbalance (right number) stacked buy shelf stacked sell shelf bar point of control value area · VPOC line zone held zone broken zone untested ▲ ABS / EXH / CAP turn — outline watching, solid ✓ confirmed, grey ✕ failed · dashed line = level it must hold scroll = zoom bars · shift+scroll (or over the price axis) = zoom price · drag = pan both · double-click = reset
📈 CHART puts these same bars in the chart engine. Same fpBuild output, same tick grouping, drawn as a custom series inside TradingView's Lightweight Charts: wheel to zoom, drag to pan, a real price axis and a crosshair that reads both scales. Each bar keeps its rows — volume that hit the bid on the left, volume that lifted the offer on the right — shaded against the heaviest cell in view, with diagonal imbalances outlined, the bar's point of control boxed, the session VPOC and any live call's levels as price lines, and turns marked. Numbers appear once bars are wide enough to read; below that the shading carries the shape.

It now carries what CELLS carries. Stacked-imbalance shelves, each bar's value-area strip and point of control, the POC path bar over bar, structure zones, the profile down the right edge in volume or delta as the PROFILE select asks, control shifts, turns, the delta row with each bar's closing delta, its volume and the track delta ran while the bar formed (the give-back), and cumulative delta in its own pane. Every one of the card's switches — Delta path, CVD, Shifts, Zones, VPOC line, Turns, PRICE STEP, IMBALANCE, STACK, PROFILE — drives this view too, so the two can never show different things. What stays behind in CELLS: the freehand drawing tools, the zone hit-and-miss states, unfinished auctions, and the hover readout panel.

Where a turn is stopped. A turn in WATCH is invalidated at its extreme. A CONFIRMED turn is stopped at the swing the confirmation built — the extreme of the bars between the turn and its confirmation — because confirmation moves the entry away from the extreme while leaving the stop behind it, which is what pushed risk to 2–8% and made a 2R target need a 4–16% move. Both geometries are logged to the Outcome Tracker as separate signals (✓ and ✓ wide), so the record decides which is worth trading instead of me.

Who, and where it turns. Every print is sorted into small, medium or large by this pair's own size distribution (bottom 50%, 50–95%, top 5%), and checked against what the book displayed at that exact price. Volume that traded beyond the displayed size means the passive side kept refilling: that is the hidden absorber. Liquidations are filed into the bar they hit. At every new 8-bar high or low the panel weighs absorption, exhaustion, hidden refills, forced flow, size-group divergence and CVD divergence, then follows the turn: watch until a reclaim or delta flip confirms it within 4 bars, failed if the extreme trades through first. Large prints are not assumed to be smart money — informed flow usually hides in medium and small prints — so the Who is moving price box measures which size group price has actually been following.

Left number is volume that hit the bid; right number is volume that lifted the offer. Both in USD, at that exact price, inside that bar. The figure under each column is the bar's delta — buys minus sells — with total traded volume beneath it. A candle chart throws all of this away and keeps four numbers.

Why it changes where the stop goes. A sweep and a reversal look identical on a candle: both print a long wick into a low. Here they do not. If the low prints heavy selling and the bar closes with delta still negative, sellers were simply getting filled and nothing has changed. If the low prints heavy selling and delta comes out positive, those sellers were absorbed and buyers took control at the bottom. The evidence sits at the low itself, so the stop goes just under that low rather than under the whole swing — the same trade at a fraction of the risk. Entering on the sweep instead means guessing; entering on the delta flip means waiting for the buyers to show up.

Imbalances are read diagonally, and that is not a detail. A limit order sits at one price. Buyers lifting the offer at P are trading against sellers resting at P; sellers hitting the bid at P are trading against buyers resting at P−1. So the meaningful comparison is buy volume at P against sell volume at P+1 — the two sides of the same queue. Comparing the two numbers printed on the same row measures nothing, because they were never facing each other. The ratio control sets how lopsided a pair has to be before it is marked.

Stacked imbalances are the boxes. One imbalanced level is noise. Three or more consecutive is a shelf of orders that got run over in one direction, and price tends to react when it comes back to it — a green box under price is a demand shelf, a red box above is supply. The gold outline on each column is that bar's point of control, the price that traded most.

The track under each delta figure is the path delta took inside the bar. Its ends are the furthest delta ran either way while the bar was forming; the notch is where it closed, and the faint tick is zero. A long track with the notch back near the middle is the give-back — the side that was pressing could not keep what it took — and it turns amber once more than 45% of the best excursion was handed back. A bar closing at +20K having been +180K on the way is not mildly bullish, and the closing figure alone hides that completely. It costs nothing to show, because the ten-second bars underneath every column already exist.

The lane at the bottom is cumulative delta across what is on screen, with the starting level as the dashed reference. It answers the question no single bar can: is all this aggression actually adding up. When price and CVD disagree at an edge — a lower low in price against a higher low in delta — the divergence is labelled in words, because an unlabelled line crossing another line explains nothing.

Small amber brackets sit at bar extremes where the auction never finished — buyers and sellers were still arguing when price left, and price tends to come back and settle it. A finished extreme prints one side only. This is stricter than the textbook definition, which counts any two-sided extreme and so fires on nearly every bar; here the two sides have to be genuinely balanced and the row has to carry real size, so the mark stays rare enough to be worth looking at.

A tinted column with a SHIFT chip marks where control changed hands. Not one bar — a sequence: a bar that spent heavily and got nothing or gave back what it took, followed within one bar by opposite delta that actually travels. Absorption alone is a defended level; expansion alone is continuation; it is absorption then expansion the other way that changes who is in charge. Thresholds are measured against the surrounding bars rather than fixed, so a quiet coin and BTC are judged the same way. Each of these three layers has its own toggle, because a chart that shows everything at once shows nothing.

Zones are drawn, and then judged. Order blocks, fair-value gaps, liquidity sweeps and untapped swing highs and lows — these are shapes until something trades at them. The shape says where price might react; only the volume at that price says whether anyone defended it. A gap price falls straight through with sellers in control was never a zone; the identical-looking gap where buying turned up and absorbed the selling was. The bands here come from the same structure map the Entry Gate builds, so a zone marked on this chart is the same zone the gate is trading — what this adds is the measurement.

An order block here is the last opposing candle before a displacement that broke structure — the final down-close bar before the move that closed through a prior swing high, and the mirror for a bearish one. That bar is where the side that lost was still being filled, and unfilled size tends to sit at the price it was working. Both tests are required: the candle after it has to displace, with a body at least 1.2× the recent average range, and that displacement has to close through the opposing swing point. A big candle that takes out nothing is just a big candle; a close through a level on a doji is drift. Blocks are read off the 15m series, not the 1m — a block worth marking is one left by a structural move, not by every large minute candle.

Mitigation is tracked separately from validation, because they answer different questions. A block price has already traded back into is mitigated and mostly spent; one price has not returned to is live. Whether it is worth anything is what the footprint decides: mitigated says price came back, HELD says somebody defended it when it did.

Each band carries how much traded inside it across the visible bars and which side was the aggressor. HELD — the side the zone favours was the net aggressor inside it. SOLD THROUGH or BOUGHT THROUGH — the other side was, which is the useful case, because it is the zone you would otherwise still be waiting at. CONTESTED — traded heavily, neither side won. UNTESTED, drawn dashed — nothing has traded there, so it remains a hypothesis rather than a level.

The candle is drawn properly now, body and wick, in its own gutter to the left of the figures rather than as a hairline through them — so whether a bar opened low and closed high can be read at the same time as its order flow, without either obscuring the other. Every cell also carries a size bar behind its figure, growing out from the centre divider, and the dominant side of each cell is set solid while the quieter side is muted. The profile of a bar should be visible as a shape before a single number is read.

The profile on the right is the tape, not a proxy. The liquidity map's profile is built from kline taker volume on whatever interval that panel happens to be set to; this one is the exact per-price data the cells above are drawn from, so the point of control it reports is the same number the columns show. Switch it to Delta and the bars become net aggression by price — which prices the window as a whole bought or sold, rather than how busy they were. A price that traded heavily with balanced delta and one that traded heavily with buyers pressing look identical on a volume profile and opposite on a delta profile.

Value area is the 70% of volume around the point of control — where business was done, as opposed to the tails price visited and left. It is drawn three ways: as a faint band across the whole window, as the dashed composite POC line, and as a short accent down the right edge of each column for that bar's own area. That last one is the useful one: two bars with the same close and the same range are different trades depending on whether their value sits at the high or the low, and a candle chart cannot show you which.

The VPOC line joins each bar's point of control. Climbing bar over bar is acceptance at higher prices; pinned in place while price probes away from it is a market that keeps getting pulled back to the same number.

It navigates like the liquidity map. Scroll to zoom the bars, shift-scroll (or scroll over the price axis) to zoom price, drag to pan both, double-click to reset. FOLLOW keeps the last trade centred; dragging or zooming price releases it, and RESET VIEW turns it back on. The price band auto-fits everything the visible bars traded, but only while the rows stay tall enough to hold two figures — past that it keeps as many rows as fit and centres on the last trade. Zoom out further and the cells become a bid-against-ask heat column: the same numbers drawn instead of written, so a wide view still reads rather than going blank. Widening PRICE STEP is the other way to fit more range with the figures intact.

What this is built from, and its limits. Binance aggTrade, which is executed volume with a real aggressor flag — measured, not inferred. But aggTrade batches same-price fills from one taker order into a single print, so counts are aggregated rather than order-by-order. Bars are accumulated at a ten-second base, so every timeframe here is an exact sum of the same prints; the price step likewise. History starts when you connect and holds about three hours. Volumes are USD notional, not contracts, so pairs are comparable to each other.

Bars are bucketed on the exchange's own trade timestamp, not on arrival. The two are not the same, and on the REST fallback they are not even close: one poll delivers up to a second and a half of prints at once, so stamping them locally would collapse that window to a single instant and file trades into whichever bar happened to be open. Prints are also deduped by aggregate-trade id on both the socket and the poller, which is what stops a socket-to-REST handover counting the same trades twice.

The price grid is a whole multiple of the pair's real tick size, read from exchangeInfo. A step invented from price alone puts row boundaries where trading cannot happen, which splits one price across two rows and manufactures an imbalance either side of it.

The badge turns DEGRADED the moment this tape stops being complete, and says why: the socket has fallen back to polling, prints went missing between polls, late prints were dropped, or the level cap was hit. A footprint that quietly loses volume still draws a convincing picture, so nothing here is allowed to fail silently.

HOW TO READ THIS CHART

Cyan / teal — a moderate cluster of positions. Some stops sit here, but not enough to attract a targeted sweep.
Yellow-green — high density. Many traders entered at prices that liquidate here. The level is starting to look attractive for a stop hunt.
Orange — very high concentration, especially 10–25× positions. Assume larger participants can see this cluster too.
Bright red — the densest cluster on the chart. Price is most likely to be driven here before reversing. This is where a stop hunt targets.
White circles (right edge) — real liquidations arriving now. Bigger circle = bigger event. Pink outline = long liquidated, cyan = short liquidated.
Dashed lines with a price tag — clusters the code detected as actual peaks, not just coloured pixels. The percentage is strength relative to the strongest cluster on screen. ▲ sits above price, ▼ below. Listed under the chart too.
Streaks that stop — a band ends where price traded through it. Those positions were liquidated; that fuel is spent. Bands still running to the right edge are live.
Tested vs untested — a dashed cluster line means price has never traded there in the visible window: that liquidity is still sitting, unclaimed. A solid line means price has been there, and the pips along it show exactly which bars, with a ring on the most recent. Several pips on one level means price keeps returning and the level keeps holding — a genuine battleground rather than a modelled guess.
Using it: find the brightest band nearest current price. Below price → longs are the fuel for a downside sweep. Above price → shorts are the fuel for an upside squeeze. The reversal after the sweep is the entry, not the sweep itself. These levels are modelled from candle closes and standard leverage tiers, not exchange position data — treat them as a map of probable clusters, not a certainty.

Hit rate by cluster intensity — does red actually mean anything?
Collecting liquidations. Every real liquidation that arrives is scored against the clusters predicted before it happened.
How the score works. When a real liquidation arrives on the !forceOrder stream, its price is compared to the nearest cluster the model had already predicted — a forward test, never fitted after the fact. The baseline runs the same measurement against the same number of levels spread evenly across the same price range. Evenly, not randomly — the model already spaces its clusters apart, so a random baseline would bunch up, cover less ground, and hand the model a large edge for spacing alone even when its placement predicts nothing. An evenly spread baseline has the same coverage, so any edge above it can only come from putting levels in the right places. If the model is not clearly beating it, the bands are not adding information and you should not lean on them. Only liquidations inside the visible price band are scored, since clusters off-screen were never predicted. Binance throttles the liquidation stream to roughly one order per symbol per second, so this is a sample, not the whole tape.

Two measured layers on one price axis. Left is resting liquidity — real limit orders sitting in the book right now, green where bids dominate, red where asks do. It is drawn from the 500-level snapshot and is always there, whether or not anything has been liquidated.

Right is real liquidations — pink longs force-sold, cyan shorts force-bought. Every event is plotted regardless of size; the scale is set by the largest cluster so small ones stay visible. Nothing here is inferred from leverage tiers.

A price with bars on both sides is the one to watch — liquidity was taken there before, and there is size sitting there again.

Every bar here is a liquidation that actually happened. Nothing is inferred from leverage tiers — these are real fills off the !forceOrder stream, bucketed by the price they executed at. Pink is longs being force-sold, cyan is shorts being force-bought.

The grey outline is where resting liquidity is sitting right now — real orders from the 500-level book, at the same price scale. So the coloured bars are where liquidity was taken, and the grey is where it is. A price with both is a level that has already been fought over and is being defended again.

Where the history comes from. With the collector running, this reads its recorded 36 hours. Without it, the browser only knows liquidations since you connected — the badge says which, and it never pretends to have more than it does. Binance throttles the stream to roughly one order per symbol per second, so totals are a floor.

HOW TO READ IT

POC (gold) — the price with the most traded volume in the window. The fairest price both sides agreed on. Price returns to it far more often than chance, which makes it the highest-probability magnet on the chart.
Value Area (blue band) — where 70% of the volume traded. Inside it the market is balanced and mean-reverting; outside it the market is trending and one side is in control.
Fat bars = HVN (high volume node) — heavily traded, so price slows and chops there. Good targets, bad places to expect a clean break.
Thin bars = LVN (low volume node) — barely traded, so price moves through fast. Good places to expect acceleration, bad places to expect support.
This is measured, not modelled — every bar is real traded volume from Binance klines, split into aggressive buying and selling using taker-buy data. Volume distribution inside each candle is approximated across its high-low range, which is standard practice; the shape is accurate, individual ticks are not.

Resolved — what happened when each wall disappeared
Nothing has resolved yet this session.
The test is simple and it is measured, not inferred. A wall that disappears because trades ate it was real size someone wanted filled. A wall that disappears with almost nothing traded at that price was cancelled — it was never for sale. FILLED means executed volume accounted for most of it. PULLED means it vanished essentially untraded. ICEBERG is the strongest accumulation signal here: the wall was eaten and immediately replaced at the same price, repeatedly — someone is working a large order and does not want you to see its true size.

Limits worth knowing. Depth is sampled once a second, so a wall placed and pulled inside that window is invisible. Trades are attributed to a level by price proximity — the exchange never tells you which order filled — so a different participant trading at the same price counts toward it. And a displayed size is only what the trader chose to show.
